influences/week-and-calendar/name: The Julian calendar, the planetary week and Anno Domini
influences/week-and-calendar/sourceCultu: Julius Caesar's solar calendar (45 BC), Roman month names and the astrological planetary week
influences/week-and-calendar/christianFo: The church year computed on the Julian (later Gregorian) calendar, weekday and month names kept or renamed, and years counted Anno Domini
influences/week-and-calendar/evidenceNot: This borrowing is beyond dispute. The Christian West and East adopted the Roman civil calendar of Julius Caesar, including month names honouring Janus, Mars, Julius and Augustus. They also adopted the planetary week, whose day names in English honour Saturn, the Sun, the Moon, and Tiw, Woden, Thunor and Frige. Christians modified rather than replaced this system. They added the Jewish-Christian seven-day framework, renamed days in Greek, Latin and Portuguese usage, created the Easter computus, and introduced Anno Domini dating (Dionysius Exiguus, 525; popularised by Bede).
influences/week-and-calendar/popularClai: Our calendar is pagan, with days and months named after gods, and the church either invented the calendar or was too compromised to change it.
influences/week-and-calendar/whatHistori: The calendar is a clear example of Christianity absorbing a civic form without importing pagan belief. Julius Caesar's reform, advised by the astronomer Sosigenes, took effect in 45 BC. The planetary week fused the Jewish seven-day cycle with Hellenistic astrology and was widespread by the second century. Christians kept the Roman months but used ecclesiastical numbering of days in the liturgy (feria secunda for Monday and so on). Martin of Braga (c.574) urged Christians not to name days after 'demons', which is why Portuguese still says segunda-feira. Anno Domini was devised by the monk Dionysius Exiguus in 525 for his Easter tables. Bede's Ecclesiastical History (731) spread it, and he also dated events 'before the incarnation'. Gregory XIII's reform of 1582 corrected the Julian drift but was resisted by Protestant and Orthodox states.
influences/week-and-calendar/summary: Christians inherited the Roman civil calendar and the astrological planetary week, along with their pagan month and day names. They overlaid them with the Easter computus, liturgical numbering of days and the Anno Domini era, a strongly attested case of adapting a civic form.
influences/week-and-calendar/story:
Julius Caesar's calendar reform of 46–45 BC replaced the chaotic Roman lunar-solar calendar with a 365-day year and a leap day every fourth year. Its months kept their old names: Ianuarius for Janus, Martius for Mars, Maius and Iunius perhaps for Maia and Juno, and the renamed Iulius and Augustus for the dictator and his heir. Christianity grew up inside this system. When bishops calculated Easter, dated councils or recorded martyrs' feasts, they used Julian dates. They also used the Roman way of counting days back from the Kalends, Nones and Ides, as in 'VIII kal. Ian.' for 25 December.

The seven-day week reached Rome from two directions. One was the Jewish Sabbath cycle, carried by diaspora synagogues and then by Christians. The other was Hellenistic astrology, which assigned each hour to one of the seven 'planets' and named each day after the planet ruling its first hour. Pompeian graffiti and Cassius Dio (37.18) show this planetary week spreading in the first and second centuries. The Christian Lord's Day thus fell on the day of the Sun and the Jewish Sabbath on Saturn's day. In Germanic languages the gods were translated: Mars into Tiw (Tuesday), Mercury into Woden (Wednesday), Jupiter into Thunor (Thursday), Venus into Frige (Friday).

Some Christians objected. The Latin liturgy numbered the weekdays as feriae, from Sunday as dies dominica through feria secunda to feria sexta, with Saturday as sabbatum. Martin of Braga, in his sermon De correctione rusticorum (c.574), denounced naming days after Mars, Mercury, Jupiter and Venus, 'who were wicked people'. Portuguese alone among major European languages adopted the ecclesiastical numbering. Charlemagne tried to give the months Frankish names (Einhard, Life of Charlemagne 29), and Quakers from the 1650s spoke of 'First Day' and 'First Month' to avoid heathen names. Most churches, however, regarded the names as harmless.

The Christian era itself came from Easter tables. In 525 Dionysius Exiguus, a Scythian monk in Rome, extended Cyril of Alexandria's Easter cycle. He replaced the era of Diocletian, a persecutor, with years counted 'from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ'. Bede adopted these anni Domini in his Reckoning of Time (725) and Ecclesiastical History (731). He also counted backwards 'before the time of the Lord's incarnation', and through Carolingian scholarship AD dating became standard across Latin Europe. The modern 'Common Era' (CE/BCE) keeps the same numbering.

The Julian year was about 11 minutes too long, so by the sixteenth century the equinox had drifted ten days. Gregory XIII's bull Inter gravissimas (1582), based on the work of Aloysius Lilius and Christopher Clavius, dropped ten days and refined the leap-year rule. Catholic countries adopted it at once. Protestant states followed between 1700 and 1752 (Britain), and most Orthodox countries changed their civil calendars only after 1917–23. Many Orthodox churches still compute Pascha on the Julian calendar, and Jerusalem, Russia, Serbia and Mount Athos keep the old calendar for fixed feasts too. A Roman pagan civic calendar thus became one of the main sources of division between Christian traditions.
influences/week-and-calendar/howItHappen: Julius Caesar's solar calendar (45 BC) became the civil framework of the Roman world in which the church grew.
The planetary week spread across the empire and merged with the Jewish-Christian seven-day cycle.
The church overlaid Roman dating with an Easter computus (Nicaea 325; Alexandrian tables; Dionysius Exiguus).
Dionysius Exiguus introduced Anno Domini (525), and Bede made it standard in the West (725–731).
Gregory XIII's reform (1582) created the Gregorian calendar. Orthodox churches kept the Julian Paschalion.
influences/week-and-calendar/examples/0: Month names honouring Janus, Mars, Juno, Julius Caesar and Augustus.
influences/week-and-calendar/examples/1: English Tuesday–Friday named after Germanic gods equated with Mars, Mercury, Jupiter and Venus.
influences/week-and-calendar/examples/2: Portuguese segunda-feira, terça-feira: the church's ferial numbering kept in a vernacular.
influences/week-and-calendar/examples/3: Bede's Ecclesiastical History (731), the first major history dated Anno Domini.
influences/week-and-calendar/examples/4: Gregory XIII's bull Inter gravissimas (1582); the Orthodox Julian Paschalion.
influences/week-and-calendar/defenders/0: Mastered Roman and Anglo-Saxon time-reckoning, explained the pagan month names and spread Anno Domini dating.
influences/week-and-calendar/defenders/1: Built Christian chronology on the Roman, Greek and Jewish systems in his Chronicle, laying the basis for a Christian world history.
influences/week-and-calendar/defenders/2: Explained Roman month and day names and their pagan origins in his Etymologies (5.30–33) as useful knowledge for Christians.
influences/week-and-calendar/critics/0/t: In De correctione rusticorum (c.574) condemned naming days after pagan gods and urged ecclesiastical numbering.
influences/week-and-calendar/critics/1/t: From the 1650s refused 'heathen' day and month names, using 'First Day' and 'First Month' instead.
influences/week-and-calendar/critics/2/t: Reject the Revised Julian (1923) and Gregorian calendars as innovations, keeping the Julian calendar for all feasts.
influences/week-and-calendar/keptBy/0: All mainstream churches (Roman month names and the planetary week in civil use)
influences/week-and-calendar/keptBy/1: Catholic and Protestant churches on the Gregorian calendar
influences/week-and-calendar/keptBy/2: Orthodox churches on the Julian Paschalion (and some on the full Julian calendar)
influences/week-and-calendar/rejectedBy/: Quakers (traditional plain speech for days and months)
Portuguese and liturgical Latin usage (pagan weekday names)
influences/mithras-and-jesus-myth/name: Mithras, Horus and the ‘copycat Christ’ claims
influences/mithras-and-jesus-myth/source: The Roman cult of Mithras, the Egyptian myth of Isis, Osiris and Horus, and other saviour figures
influences/mithras-and-jesus-myth/christ: Claimed source of the Gospel story of Jesus — virgin birth, 25 December, twelve disciples, death and resurrection
influences/mithras-and-jesus-myth/eviden: No ancient source describes Mithras or Horus as born of a virgin on 25 December, having twelve disciples, being crucified or rising after three days; Roman Mithraism is attested only from the late first century, after the earliest Christian writings.
influences/mithras-and-jesus-myth/popula: Jesus never existed or was modelled on earlier gods: Mithras and Horus were both born of a virgin on 25 December, had twelve disciples, performed miracles, were crucified and rose on the third day, so Christianity copied them wholesale.
influences/mithras-and-jesus-myth/whatHi: These lists derive from nineteenth-century writers such as Gerald Massey and Kersey Graves (The World’s Sixteen Crucified Saviors, 1875), revived by Acharya S (D. M. Murdock) and the film Zeitgeist (2007). Specialists in Roman Mithraism (Manfred Clauss, Roger Beck, Richard Gordon) and Egyptologists find no support: Mithras is born from a rock, fully grown; he kills a bull and banquets with Sol; he does not die or rise. Horus is conceived by Isis from the reassembled Osiris; he has no twelve disciples and is not crucified. The cult of Mithras is attested from c. AD 80–100, so if anything it is later than Paul’s letters. Historians, including sceptics such as Bart Ehrman, regard the ‘copycat’ thesis as unfounded.
influences/mithras-and-jesus-myth/summar: A popular internet claim holds that Jesus is a copy of Mithras, Horus and other gods. The evidence does not support it; the real story is of two cults that grew up side by side in the Roman Empire, shared some broad religious language, and were noticed by Christian writers at the time.
influences/mithras-and-jesus-myth/story:
The Roman cult of Mithras was a mystery cult for men, popular among soldiers, imperial officials and merchants from the late first to the late fourth century. Its members met in small, cave-like sanctuaries (mithraea) for a shared meal, progressed through seven grades of initiation (Raven to Father), and venerated an image of Mithras slaying a bull, flanked by two torch-bearers, Cautes and Cautopates. Hundreds of mithraea are known, from Hadrian’s Wall to the Danube; one survives beneath the basilica of San Clemente in Rome. The cult borrowed the name of the Persian god Mithra, but most scholars since the 1970s (Gordon, Ulansey, Beck) see it as a new Roman creation rather than a continuation of Iranian religion, as Franz Cumont had argued in the 1890s.

The ‘copycat’ claims do not match the sources. Mithras is born from a rock (petra genetrix), not a virgin. The date 25 December appears in the Roman Chronograph of 354 as the birthday of the Unconquered Sun (Natalis Invicti), with whom Mithras was sometimes identified in dedications, but no ancient text assigns 25 December to Mithras’s birth, and the Christian date has other proposed explanations (see the entry on the date of Christmas). Mithras has no twelve disciples — the twelve signs of the zodiac appear in some reliefs — and there is no death, burial or resurrection in his story. For Horus, the Egyptian myth tells of Isis reassembling the murdered Osiris and conceiving their son; there is no virgin birth, baptism, twelve followers or crucifixion in ancient Egyptian texts.

There were real points of contact. Justin Martyr (1 Apology 66; Dialogue 70, 78) and Tertullian (Prescription against Heretics 40) noted that Mithraists shared bread and water, marked initiates on the forehead and told of a birth in a cave; they attributed these to demonic imitation. This shows that Christians knew of the cult and resented the comparison, which hardly suggests they had copied it. The direction of any influence is uncertain, and since the cult flourished after Christianity was established, some influence from Christianity on Mithraism cannot be ruled out. Both cults also drew on common Roman religious language: sacred meals, light and solar imagery, and initiation.

The modern claims have a traceable history. Enlightenment writers such as Charles-François Dupuis (1795) reduced Christ to a solar myth; Gerald Massey (1880s) and Kersey Graves (1875) produced the lists of parallels; and D. M. Murdock’s The Christ Conspiracy (1999) and the online film Zeitgeist (2007) spread them widely. Historians across the religious spectrum, including agnostics such as Bart Ehrman in Did Jesus Exist? (2012), reject them for lack of evidence. The cult of Mithras declined in the late fourth century, when Theodosius I’s laws of 391–392 banned pagan sacrifice, and some mithraea were destroyed or built over by churches.

A fair conclusion is that Christianity and Mithraism were contemporaries competing in the same world, sharing some symbolic idioms, but that the specific claims of copied biographies are modern inventions.
influences/mithras-and-jesus-myth/howItH: Roman Mithraism arose in the late first century and spread through the army and imperial administration.
Second-century Christians noticed some ritual similarities and explained them as demonic counterfeits.
Eighteenth- and nineteenth-century writers built ‘solar myth’ theories and lists of parallels without ancient citations.
Late twentieth-century authors and the internet revived these lists, especially through the film Zeitgeist (2007).
Specialist historians of Roman religion and Egyptologists have repeatedly found the claims unsupported.
influences/mithras-and-jesus-myth/exampl: The Mithraeum beneath San Clemente in Rome, with its bull-slaying relief.
The tauroctony (bull-slaying) reliefs of Mithras with Cautes and Cautopates.
Justin Martyr’s remark on Mithraic bread and water (1 Apology 66).
The Chronograph of 354, listing 25 December as Natalis Invicti.
Kersey Graves, The World’s Sixteen Crucified Saviors (1875), source of many modern lists.
influences/mithras-and-jesus-myth/critic: Treated the Mithraic meal and cave as demonic imitations of Christian rites and prophecy.
Described Mithraic initiation as the devil’s mimicry of the sacraments (Prescription against Heretics 40).
Agnostic New Testament scholar who examined and rejected the ‘copycat’ and ‘Christ myth’ claims in Did Jesus Exist? (2012).
Historian of Roman Mithraism whose survey of the evidence shows none of the alleged parallels in the ancient sources.

influences/mithras-and-jesus-myth/reject: Historians of Roman religion and Egyptologists
New Testament scholars of all persuasions, religious and secular
